text: Sweden spent years building a giant warship. It sailed for about twenty minutes.
Sixty-four guns. Two gun decks. Hundreds of painted sculptures.
The King had approved the design himself.
But before it sailed, they tested it.
About thirty men ran back and forth across the deck.
The ship rocked so hard, they feared it would capsize right there at the dock.
So they stopped the test.
And sent it out anyway.
Sunday, August tenth, sixteen twenty-eight. Four sails up. A cannon salute.
A light breeze.
Then one gust.
The Vasa leaned over, and water poured in through the open gunports.
It sank about thirteen hundred metres out. At least thirty people died.
You see, a ship stays upright like a punching-bag toy: heavy at the bottom, so it always rolls back up.
The Vasa's tall decks and heavy guns put too much weight up high.
So one gust was enough.
There was an inquiry. Who was to blame?
Officially, nobody.
Most of the blame quietly landed on the shipbuilder, who had died the year before.
In nineteen sixty-one, the Vasa was raised. Today it's ninety-eight percent original.
As a warship, it lasted about twenty minutes. As a museum, it's been packed for over thirty years.
